newsitem.title: UK: Pearson seen keeping TV, Tussauds.
newsitem.headline: Pearson seen keeping TV, Tussauds.

text.p: Media and leisure group Pearson Plc is unlikely to sell either its television unit or its Tussauds tourist attractions, analysts said on Monday.
"It appears the disposals are not going to be television or Tussauds," said SocGen analyst Jason Crisp.
In separate briefings to analysts and journalists, Pearson chief executive Marjorie Scardino referred to television as "the fastest growing" of any of the company's businesses.
She also spoke of the need to invest in the Tussauds Group, which includes the Madame Tussaud's wax museum and theme parks such as Alton Towers in the UK and Port Aventura in Spain.
Scardino, who took over as chief executive in January, would not specify which businesses Pearson planned to sell as part of the drive for focus.
She did say that Pearson was looking at its stakes in companies where it does not have a majority stake.
"I take that to mean that Lazards must go as that is not a managed business," said Nick Ward of Credit Lyonnais Laing.

Pearson has a 50 percent stake in London merchant bank Lazard Brothers plus smaller holdings in Lazard Freres operations in New York and Paris. The Lazard houses contributed almost 41 million stg to Pearson's 1996 profit.

Ward said he believed that Pearson may also seek to sell its remaining indirect holding in satellite broadcaster BSkyB. It has a stake of around four percent in BSkyB which it owns through BSB Holdings Limited.

Pearson shares were off 14p at 760p by 1605 GMT on Monday and one analyst said that there was some disappointment that the new management had not made clear what its core businesses were likely to be.
"It still seems to be a case of trying to advance on all fronts. Meanwhile there is a problem with cash," said one, noting dividend cover of just 1.7 times.
Analysts were rather sceptical about plans to expand the Financial Times internationally through a 100 million stg investment programme over five years.
Some expressed frustration that it was not made clear how that investment was going to be capitalised while others noted that the FT faced tough competition in the US from the Wall Street Journal.
The general impression was that the Pearson presentation was a little short on specifics and that it would take time to assess the quality of the new management
"We're slightly in limbo land," said Ward of Credit Lyonnais Laing.
